sentences.text: Delapparentia was a large iguanodont dinosaur that lived in Spain during the Early Cretaceous, reaching lengths of roughly ten meters and weighing about 3.5 tonnes.

Its skeleton featured a 78-centimeter-long ilium with a straight, lateromedially expanded preacetabular process, alongside unique posterior dorsal ribs with long, parallel, unfused ends and ossified sternal ribs.
New remains revealed proportionally high neural spines, leading researchers to relate the species to the earlier Barilium from England based on ilium morphology.
The generic name honors Albert Félix de Lapparent, who published the first monograph on Spanish dinosaurs, while the specific name comes from the Latin name of Teruel, Turia.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — is a partial adult skeleton lacking a skull but containing numerous vertebrae, rib fragments, and a left pubis and ilium.

Amateur paleontologist José María Herrero Marzo found the type specimen in the spring of 1958, after which Professor Dimas Fernández-Galiano collected it with a Dutch team starting September 25, 1958.

Albert-Félix de Lapparent originally assigned the finds to Iguanodon bernissartensis in 1960, and some bones he misidentified as belonging to the sauropod Aragosaurus were later referred to Delapparentia.
José Ignacio Ruiz-Omeñaca validly named the genus Delapparentia turolensis in a 2011 paper after initially naming it in a 2006 dissertation.
Ruiz-Omeñaca assigned Delapparentia to the Iguanodontoidea in 2011.

Delapparentia turolensis lived during the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 130 million years ago, with a time range estimated from 125.77 to 121.4 million years ago in what is now Europe.
Some researchers challenge the identification of Delapparentia as a distinct taxon, suggesting it represents an old adult individual of Iguanodon bernissartensis based on neural spine proportions.
